How to recognise it: Across more than one evenly lit view, the skin may read more golden, yellow, or peach than rosy or bluish.
What to observe: Compare the jaw, upper chest, and the less-exposed inner arm; note the repeated cast rather than a temporary flush.
How it differs from a nearby label: Unlike surface redness, an undertone is the background cast that can still be noticed when short-term redness settles.
What the observation means: Record it as a working observation only. It describes a repeated cast, not a fixed identity or a judgement about depth.

How to recognise it: Across more than one evenly lit view, the skin may read more rosy, pink, or bluish than golden or yellow.
What to observe: Check the jaw, upper chest, and inner arm in the same light before deciding from cheeks alone.
How it differs from a nearby label: Unlike a temporary rosy surface, this label is for a cast that appears in several areas and at more than one time.
What the observation means: Record it as a working observation; it is not a diagnosis and does not require a product choice.

How to recognise it: No clearly warm or clearly cool cast stays dominant across the areas and lighting conditions you compare.
What to observe: Look for a balance or for the answer to change slightly between jaw, neck, and inner arm.
How it differs from a nearby label: Unlike uncertainty from poor light, neutral-leaning is a repeatable lack of one dominant warm or cool cast in usable light.
What the observation means: Use it when the evidence stays balanced. It is an observation label, not a demand to force a more specific answer.

How to recognise it: A muted green-grey or yellow-green cast may be noticeable alongside warm, cool, or neutral features.
What to observe: Observe the jaw and neck in daylight and compare them with the inner arm; avoid judging from a strongly coloured wall or screen light.
How it differs from a nearby label: Unlike simply being deeper or lighter in depth, this describes a muted cast. It can overlap with warm, cool, or neutral-leaning observations.
What the observation means: Write it as an additional note rather than treating it as a separate, exclusive category.

How to recognise it: Depth describes how light or deep an area appears, independently of whether its cast seems warm, cool, neutral, or olive-leaning.
What to observe: Compare areas on the same person in the same light; do not use a screen image with an unknown exposure as the main reference.
How it differs from a nearby label: Unlike undertone, depth is about apparent lightness or darkness, not whether the background cast reads golden, rosy, balanced, or muted.
What the observation means: Use depth as a descriptive note only. There is no authority-backed numerical cut-off on this page.

How to recognise it: One area may look redder, duller, darker, or more shadowed than the surrounding skin without changing the underlying cast everywhere else.
What to observe: Check cheeks, around the nose, under the jaw, and any area affected by recent sun, heat, pressure, hair removal, or shadows.
How it differs from a nearby label: Unlike an undertone, a surface change can be local, temporary, or direction-dependent when the light moves.
What the observation means: Keep this in a separate note so it does not overwrite the undertone observation.

How to recognise it: Face, neck, chest, and arms do not give one neat answer, or different areas consistently show different surface conditions.
What to observe: Write each area separately: for example, jaw cast, cheek surface colour, neck cast, and inner-arm reference.
How it differs from a nearby label: This is not a failed classification. It differs from a single-label reading because the disagreement itself is the useful observation.
What the observation means: Use a combined record instead of forcing every area into one consumer label.
